title: November 2026 - Liberty Street Economics
gist: A November 2026 Liberty Street Economics index page previews a post by Correia, Luck and Verner on how supervisors handle failing banks. It argues closures rest on book-equity data that supervision partly shapes, and that stricter supervision lowers resolution costs but can restrict credit supply.

insights.claim: Bank failures typically result from supervisory closure decisions that are based on hard information about book equity, rather than from market-driven runs alone.
insights.speaker: Sergio Correia, Stephan Luck, and Emil Verner
insights.so_what: Book-equity reporting, not market signals, is the trigger to watch for bank closures.
insights.quote: bank failures typically result from supervisory closure decisions based on hard information about book equity

insights.claim: The hard book-equity information that triggers closures is itself partly produced by supervision, because supervisors require troubled banks to recognize potential losses.
insights.speaker: Sergio Correia, Stephan Luck, and Emil Verner
insights.so_what: Reported capital at troubled banks reflects supervisory pressure, so reported equity may lag or jump when supervisors push loss recognition.

insights.claim: Stricter supervision can reduce the costs of resolving failing banks.
insights.speaker: Sergio Correia, Stephan Luck, and Emil Verner
insights.so_what: Earlier, firmer intervention lowers resolution losses, which matters for deposit insurance and taxpayers.

insights.claim: Stricter supervision can also tighten regulatory capital constraints and hold back credit supply.
insights.speaker: Sergio Correia, Stephan Luck, and Emil Verner
insights.so_what: Tougher supervision of weak banks can weigh on lending and credit availability, a macro and bank-credit headwind.

insights.claim: Supervision faces a trade-off between lower resolution costs and tighter capital constraints that restrain credit supply.
insights.speaker: Sergio Correia, Stephan Luck, and Emil Verner
insights.so_what: Policy shifts toward stricter or looser supervision carry a cost-versus-credit tradeoff that bank investors should price.
